acquisition.why: Inbound channels are workable: Amazon, a Shopify store, TikTok Shop, paid social and fitness influencer affiliates. Agents can run the ads and listings, but the brand relies heavily on paid ads and marketplaces.

onboarding.why: Consumers simply check out. There is no onboarding beyond the store or marketplace flow.

delivery.why: This is physical food. It needs a co-packer, allergen controls, shelf-life management and 3PL or FBA logistics. Batches, quality checks and stock decisions all need a human.

billing.why: Shopify or Amazon payments are automated. Refunds and chargebacks need occasional checks.

support.why: Agents can answer routine questions about orders and ingredients. Allergen incidents, damaged goods and food complaints need a human, and they carry liability.

scores.R_why: A £300 budget cannot fund a minimum co-packer run, which is typically £3k–£15k+ including packaging [E]. Ricardo would also need local authority food business registration, UK nutrition and protein claim compliance (Retained Reg 1924/2006), allergen labelling and product liability insurance. Food product development is not a fit for 6–8 hours a week.
scores.M_why: UK protein-fortified foods are saturated. Grenade, Myprotein, Fulfil, Kodiak and supermarket own-label ranges all compete here, and Mr Kipling and Weetabix sell protein variants. Margins are thin, and shelf and ad costs are high.
scores.one_line: This is a crowded, capital-heavy physical food brand with regulatory exposure, and the dossier offers no figures or validation; poor fit for an agent-run £300 UK test.

acquisition.why: The YouTube channel variant sells through marketplaces like Flippa and Acquire.com, which is legal and inbound. Each sale is negotiated and needs human due diligence, though. The Instagram/Telegram variant breaches platform terms.

onboarding.why: Buyer vetting, escrow, verifying analytics and transferring channel ownership are manual and trust-heavy. YouTube's brand-account owner change has a 7-day wait.

delivery.why: Agents can draft scripts, voiceover, edits and uploads for a faceless channel. A human needs to check quality, avoid repetitive or inauthentic content strikes, and make niche decisions.

billing.why: AdSense pays out automatically while the channel is growing. The final sale goes through escrow, and the large one-off transaction needs a human.

support.why: Comment moderation can be agent-run. After the sale there are only light obligations, such as a handover period.

scores.R_why: A faceless YouTube channel can be built with agents on low cash. However, reaching monetisation (1k subs and 4k hours) and then meaningful AdSense revenue can take more than 12 months, with high variance [E]. YouTube's 2025 inauthentic and mass-produced content policy directly targets AI-churned channels. Selling Instagram accounts breaches Meta's terms. UK capital gains or trading tax would apply to any sale.
scores.M_why: AI-generated faceless channels flooded YouTube in 2025–26, and demonetisation risk is high. Buyers discount channels that depend on AI content. The Instagram account market is grey and shrinking (the speaker says the tactics no longer work).
scores.one_line: The '$3k/mo channel sells for $100k' figure is hypothetical, and AI-content faceless channels face YouTube demonetisation and buyer discounting; a slow, speculative asset play rather than an agent-run business.

acquisition.why: Airbnb listings or attraction booking sites are inbound and legal. However, the venue has to exist physically and be marketed locally, and the platform-based variant depends entirely on Airbnb.

onboarding.why: Online booking can be automated. On-site check-in, safety briefings and waivers need staff or physical setup.

delivery.why: The work is entirely physical. It involves transporting and siting the aircraft, maintaining it, cleaning it, running rides and supervising safety.

billing.why: Booking platforms and Stripe take payment automatically.

support.why: Guest issues, safety incidents and damage claims need a human on the ground.

scores.R_why: The startup cost is $322k–$500k+, roughly 1,000 times the £300 budget. GSA auctions are US-only, and shipping or importing an airframe would be extreme. The idea would also need UK planning permission, building regulations, fire safety, amusement-device inspection (ADIPS) and public liability cover. None of this is compatible with a part-time parent in Bromley.
scores.M_why: Novelty aircraft stays face little direct competition (a few UK examples such as the Hotel and Airbnb plane conversions exist [E]). Demand is niche, though, and it is a one-off property business rather than a scalable one.
scores.one_line: This is a speculative, joke-level idea ('$10 per ride') needing $500k+ of capital, US sourcing and heavy UK planning and safety regulation; entirely unsuitable.
